ingredients.h2: Three named, and a blend that is not
ingredients.intro: The listing names three plants and calls the remainder a proprietary blend. Here are the three, with the botany, the family and where each one grows. We hold no photograph of any of the three, so those frames are empty rather than filled with a stand-in, and any picture on this page that is a generated scene says so. The fourth card is the blend, written down as the gap it is.

cards.p: A woodland perennial of the eastern United States and Canada, with a tall white flowering spike that gives it the older name black snakeroot. The rhizome and root are the parts usually sold. Herbals printed before about 2000 file it as Cimicifuga racemosa, which is the same plant renamed. Which part of it is in this jar is not printed. The caution that travels with this plant is on the sheet below.

The pink-purple clover of European pasture and roadside, now naturalised across most of the temperate world and grown as fodder and as a green manure. The flower head is the part usually dried and sold. The listing does not say which part is in this jar.

A twining vine of damp woodland from the eastern United States down into Mexico, with heart-shaped leaves and a knotted underground rhizome. The rhizome is the part usually sold. It is not the yam of the greengrocer, which is a different set of Dioscorea species grown as a staple food.

cards.common: No plant in it is printed
cards.p: Whatever else is in the capsule appears on the listing as a proprietary blend and nothing further. The phrase means the label is not telling you. It is the one row on this sheet we cannot fill in, and until the label prints the plants it stays a row of nothing.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: Three plants are named here in Latin, the milligrams and the count are printed, and where the listing gives two different servings this page prints both rather than the one that reads better. Equill is the name on the jar. It is a name, not a description, and we do not expand it. What any of these plants does in a body is not something we are permitted to say, so it is not on this page.

reiss.label: Reiss's turn
reiss.h2: Why proprietary blend is a phrase I want off our labels
paras: Three plants are named on this listing and the rest of it sits behind two words. I understand why formulators reach for them. I also think they fail the only test that counts at a counter, which is whether the person holding the jar can go away and find out what is in it.

The three that are named can be looked up by anyone. You can read that Actaea racemosa is a woodland perennial of the eastern United States, find the caution that travels with it, and decide for yourself. There is no equivalent move for a blend.

The serving is printed twice on this listing and the two do not agree. I have put both on the sheet with the arithmetic for each, rather than pick the version that makes the day rate look better. Ring the shop and somebody will read you what the current label says.

The caution on this one is not a formality. Black cohosh carries a warning about the liver wherever it is sold here, and the listing's own advisory says the same thing. It sits above the small print on this page rather than under it, because that is where people actually read.
reiss.pull: Three names and a blank is not an ingredient list.
